newsitem.title: USA: Maricopa Cty,Ariz.,to consider settlement with SEC.
newsitem.headline: Maricopa Cty,Ariz.,to consider settlement with SEC.

text.p: Maricopa County, Ariz., said on Monday its Board of Supervisors would meet on October 2 to consider an offer to settle with the Securities and Exchange Commission.
In so doing, the county said it would neither admit nor deny any of the SEC's allegations.
"With the anticipated Board action, and the expected acceptance by the Commission, we consider the matter closed," the county said in a statement.
Earlier on Monday, the SEC said it instituted cease and desist proceedings against Maricopa County, the sixth largest county in the nation.
The SEC alleged that the county violated the anti-fraud provisions of the federal securities laws in connection with the July 1993 offer and sale of two series of general obligation bonds.

Maricopa County said it had cooperated fully with the SEC investigation of the bond deals. "This is a civil administrative proceeding, and no current or former county officials or employees have been charged," the county said.
The county said it has met all payment obligations on the bonds, both principal and interest, and will continue to do so, on schedule, as it has in the past.

The county said its lawyers have worked with the SEC to resolve this matter since its inception. The Board of Supervisors on October 2 will be presented with a proposed settlement, the county said. The terms of the settlement were prepared in collaboration with attorneys for the SEC.
"The county has every reasonable expectation that, if approved by the Board, the settlement will be accepted by the Commission in the very near future," the county said.
Under this settlement, the county would neither admit nor deny any of the SEC's findings. No fines or penalties would be imposed on the county.
The county said the financial problems that it faced in 1993 were addressed. Procedures to ensure SEC requirements will be met in the future are in place, the county added.

"The prospects for a healthy financial future for Maricopa County are bright and attainable," the county said. "There is nothing to gain, from the county's perspective, by engaging in protracted litigation now over events that occurred over three years ago."
